analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Ways and Means Committee: introduced January 7, 1997, referred to committee the same day, and never brought up for a House vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the federal taxes owed when large amounts of wealth are transferred — at death, as gifts, or across generations. Only estates and gifts above certain sizes ever owed these taxes, so repeal would exclusively benefit families passing on the largest fortunes. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with the largest estates and people making large taxable gifts. The estate tax only applies above an exemption amount, so the benefit is concentrated among households holding the greatest wealth, and the largest fortunes benefit the most.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, which contains the estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax [S2][S3].
The repeal would apply to the estates of people dying and to transfers made after the date of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers, because the federal government would lose the revenue these taxes raise on the largest wealth transfers, leaving other taxes or borrowing to cover the difference.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax that falls only on the largest estates and gifts, shifting the federal tax burden toward everyone else and making the tax code less progressive [S2][S3].
The generation-skipping transfer tax specifically targets a strategy for passing wealth to grandchildren while skipping a layer of taxation; repeal would remove that backstop [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a large tax cut that flows overwhelmingly to families with the biggest fortunes, while the cost is permanent revenue loss borne by taxpayers at large. Because the taxes being repealed apply only above exemption thresholds, the benefits and costs are sharply lopsided.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Pitts introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the opening day of the 105th Congress [S1][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
Six Republican members cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal estate and gift taxes remained in place, so wealthy families continued to pay them while the general Treasury kept the revenue. Committee leadership was spared a floor fight over a full repeal that had only a handful of cosponsors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and large-estate tax status quo

for.name: Rep. Joseph R. Pitts
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 105th Congress and gave introductory remarks.

for.name: 6 Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it no Democratic support.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 7, 1997 and never scheduled any action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters in the record — the sponsor and six cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored or acted on the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would have spared the largest estates and gifts from federal transfer taxes; only estates above the exemption thresholds ever owed them, so the gain concentrates at the top of the wealth distribution. The bill died, so those taxes stayed on the books.

These professionals earn fees helping clients structure estates and gifts around transfer taxes, so repeal would have shrunk part of their business. Families avoiding those same taxes would have lost the planning tools the tax regime supports.
